description: We are a team who came together to learn, build, and solve problems as a group. Our members bring different strengths: user experience and interface design, research and data verification, and backend development and SI integration. We work with a simple approach: split the work by strengths, keep communication open, and always focus on delivering something that works. We’re excited to turn ideas into a real product and to learn from every part of the experience.
summary:
What we built: A web-based explorer for NASA research on how fire behaves in microgravity. It connects real investigations aboard the International Space Station: SAME (smoke detection), BASS/BASS-II (burning solid materials) and FLEX (burning fuel droplets). It includes charts of measured data taken straight from published NASA/NIST papers, a Research Explorer with search, filters and side-by-side comparison, and an animated Mission Simulator. An AI research assistant answers only from verified evidence and says so when the evidence isn't there. There's also a Global Impact map with six educational case studies.

How it addresses the challenge: Flame in Freefall asks people to understand fire in space. IGNIS turns scattered NASA findings into clear, source-linked visuals. Every item carries one of five labels: verified measurement, published finding, qualitative observation, illustrative visualization, or missing data.

Why it matters: Fire is one of the most dangerous threats to a crewed mission. IGNIS teaches this science honestly. It never invents data or claims to predict risk, and it links lessons from space to fire safety on Earth.
details:
Our project, IGNIS — Understand the Fire. Protect the Mission, is an interactive web platform designed to make NASA's research on fire in space easier to explore and understand.

Fire behaves differently in microgravity compared to Earth, which makes understanding combustion important for future space missions. NASA has conducted several experiments to study this, but the information is spread across scientific papers, technical reports, and datasets. We noticed that finding and connecting these results can be difficult, especially for students and people who are new to the topic. That's the problem we wanted to solve.

IGNIS brings together five NASA combustion investigations: SAME, BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, and Saffire-I. Our Research Explorer includes an interactive 2.5D research map where users can explore connections between experiments and scientific topics. It also provides charts using published NASA measurements, search and filtering options, and the ability to compare investigations. Users can see the experimental conditions, original sources, and limitations rather than just looking at numbers without context.

We also created the Mission Lab, which uses interactive visual demonstrations to explain concepts such as smoke particles, flame spread, and droplet combustion in microgravity. These are educational illustrations that help users understand the research, not simulations that predict actual fire behavior.

Another important feature is IGNIS Intelligence, our AI-assisted research system. Users can ask questions about NASA combustion experiments and receive explanations connected to scientific evidence. We integrated Google Gemini to help organize information from our curated research library. Instead of allowing AI to generate unsupported scientific measurements or citations, we designed the system to use approved evidence and clearly explain what is known and what is still uncertain. It can also provide evidence-based answers without Gemini.

One of our latest additions is Global Impact. We originally started with Bahrain, but we wanted to show how IGNIS could also be useful internationally. We developed an interactive world map featuring six countries: Bahrain, the United States, Japan, India, the UAE, and Canada. Each country has its own educational case study, supported by official space-programme information, showing how NASA combustion research could help students and future researchers explore relevant scientific questions.

For Bahrain, we included an interactive educational model of Al Munther, Bahrain's satellite, along with verified mission information and an explanation of how combustion research could be relevant to future satellite engineering studies. We also included a map using official Bahrain fire-station location data and three learning activities available in both English and Arabic. The Global Impact section is also bilingual, making the information more accessible to different audiences.

We developed IGNIS using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG, and Node.js. We used NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics resources and published research reports for the scientific information, Google Gemini for optional AI assistance, and GitHub for collaboration and version control. We also used Codex and Claude Code to help with development, design, and testing. Our website is deployed using Render, allowing people to access it online.

What makes IGNIS different is that we didn't want to create another website filled with scientific text. We wanted people to interact with the research. By combining real experimental data, interactive visualizations, an AI-assisted research tool, and educational activities, we made it possible to explore complicated scientific topics in a more understandable way.

Throughout development, we focused on scientific accuracy, accessibility, user experience, and transparency. We made sure to show original sources, distinguish actual measurements from illustrations, and avoid presenting missing or unverified information as facts. We also considered how research from space can be discussed in different educational contexts without assuming that the same findings automatically apply everywhere.

Our main goal is to help bridge the gap between NASA's scientific research and the people who could benefit from understanding it. We hope IGNIS can become a useful learning and research resource for students, educators, and future space researchers around the world. While IGNIS does not predict fires or replace real spacecraft safety systems, it can help people better understand the science that may contribute to safer space exploration in the future.
